newsitem.title: USA: Dollar gains as US jobs point to higher rates.
newsitem.headline: Dollar gains as US jobs point to higher rates.

text.p: The dollar rose Friday after a surprisingly steep drop in America's jobless rate confirmed robust economic growth and boosted expectations for a near-term rise in U.S. interest rates.
Rallies in U.S. bond and stock markets also bolstered the dollar.

The United States added 250,000 new non-farm jobs in August, exceeding expectations for a 224,000 gain, while the unemployment rate fell to a seven-year-low of 5.1 percent from 5.4 percent in July, the Labour Department said Friday.
Analysts said the data showed the economy expanding at a brisk pace and increased the odds the Federal Reserve will increase interest rates this month.
"What you've got here is a pretty strong bias for a rate hike right now," said Kevin Harris, international economist at MCM CurrencyWatch.
Late Friday, the dollar rose to 109.28 Japanese yen and 1.4920 German marks from 109.20 yen and 1.4863 marks late Thursday.
The dollar initially dipped after release of the stronger-than-expected jobs data, opening at 1.4850 marks and 109.12 yen, and falling in sympathy with sinking U.S. Treasury bond prices.

But bonds and stocks, which had been heavily oversold in advance of the jobs data, soon perked up, helping the dollar rebound, as the market doubted that the economy was strong enough to prompt a half-percentage-point rise in interest rates.

The Dow Jones industrial average soared nearly 53 points to 5,659 late Friday, while the benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond was up 16/32 at 95.17-18, with the yield falling to 7.11 percent from 7.15 percent at Thursday's close.

"The (jobs) numbers lead us to think that the Federal Reserve will move in September, raising rates by 25 basis points," said Jim Phoenix, director of foreign exchange sales at the Canadian Imperial Bank of Commerce.
The Fed is widely expected to raise short-term interest rates by 0.25 percentage point when its policymaking committee, the Federal Open Market Committee, meets Sept. 24.
Higher U.S. interest rates would benefit the dollar by making assets denominated in the U.S. currency more attractive than those based in foreign currencies.
The dollar had spent most of overnight Asian trading confined to narrow ranges as the market anxiously awaited the release of U.S. jobs data.

The U.S. unit received mild support from comments by unidentified Japanese government sources that a dollar rise above 110 yen would not be a big problem or have a negative impact on the Japanese economy.

The sources also said they believed the U.S. government wanted a stronger dollar to boost investment, and that worries U.S. exporters would lose their competitive edge concerned only certain industries.
The comments were at odds with recent complaints by American carmakers that a strengtheing dollar was hurting exports by boosting the prices of U.S. goods sold overseas.
In other trading, the British pound fell to $1.5604 compared with $1.5660.
The dollar was also sharply higher at 1.2189 Swiss francs versus 1.2080 on Thursday, and eased to Canadian $1.3728 against C$1.3733.
